(CNN) -- Taliban advances in Pakistan are raising concerns in Islamabad and capitals as far away as Washington. CNN's senior international correspondent Nic Robertson looks at how the Taliban spread and what could be done to help Pakistan. Students in burqas in Buner district . But the Taliban has also extended its influence because it is now involved with several Punjab terrorist groups that have affiliated themselves with the border Taliban and have helped commit some attacks such as one on a police station in Lahore. The Pakistan government has been cutting deals with the different elements that were Taliban or became Taliban since 2004-2005. Those deals have enabled the Taliban to extend themselves. Is Pakistan going to fall or fail? The overall answer to that is no. But the Taliban is further destabilizing an incredibly unstable situation. There is a weak government that faces challenges, not only from the Taliban but also from almost every political party in the country. It faces challenges from across the border with its old enemy India, which means a large percentage of the Pakistan army is tied up on that border rather than fighting terrorism. The Taliban is not going to take Islamabad, but its attacks and advances are going to weaken an already unstable government and make an already dangerous situation even more volatile... and that will mean the Taliban will be able to wield more influence in the future than they do today. What options are open to the Pakistan government and other countries? Pakistan could form a broad-based government of national unity and appeal for more international support in terms of encouraging financial aid and having trade restrictions lifted so they can improve the economy. The international community could help Pakistan resolve issues with India. It would help the economy and help the government focus on its own internal problems and better influence the situation in Afghanistan. What the Pakistan government would also need to do is convince its people that outside support and help is in their best interests to deal with terrorism and stabilize the country. To do that the government would also have to win the support of its large Pashtun minority, from whom the Taliban draws a lot of its support ... and that is difficult particularly as the U.S. -- which would need to be a principle supporter of Pakistan -- continues to bomb targets in Pashtun areas leading to civilian casualties.

**How is the Taliban extending its influence in Pakistan?**

The Taliban has significantly expanded its influence over the past several years, advancing northward along the Pakistan-Afghanistan border—from South Waziristan to North Waziristan, then to Bajaur, and now into Swat and Buner. The group has also broadened its reach by forging ties with several militant organizations in Punjab that have aligned themselves with the border-based Taliban, contributing to attacks such as the assault on a police station in Lahore. These agreements have inadvertently allowed the Taliban to consolidate and expand its position.

**Is Pakistan at risk of collapse or failure?**

The short answer is no. However, the Taliban is exacerbating an already precarious and unstable situation. Pakistan's government is weak and confronts challenges not only from the Taliban but from nearly every political party within the country. It also faces tensions across the border with its longstanding rival, India—tensions that require a substantial portion of the Pakistani army to remain stationed there rather than engaged in counterterrorism efforts. While the Taliban is unlikely to seize control of Islamabad, its continued attacks and territorial gains will further destabilize an already fragile government, intensifying an already volatile situation. This, in turn, will grant the Taliban greater influence in the future than it currently wields.

**What options are available to the Pakistani government and the international community?**

Pakistan could establish a broad-based government of national unity and appeal to the international community for greater support—both in securing financial aid and in lifting trade restrictions to help bolster its economy. The Pakistani government must also persuade its population that accepting outside assistance serves the nation's best interests in combating terrorism and achieving stability. Achieving this will require winning the support of the country's substantial Pashtun minority, from which the Taliban draws considerable backing—a task made especially difficult given that the United States, which would need to serve as a principal source of support for Pakistan, continues to conduct strikes in Pashtun regions that result in civilian casualties.

# The Growing Taliban Threat in Pakistan: An Analysis

(CNN) -- The advancing presence of Taliban forces within Pakistan is generating anxiety not just in Islamabad but in distant capitals like Washington as well. CNN senior international correspondent Nic Robertson examines the mechanics of this expansion and possible remedies for Pakistan's predicament.

Female students wearing burqas can be seen in the Buner district as the crisis unfolds.

**How has the Taliban managed to expand its reach across Pakistan?**

Over the past several years, the militant group has steadily pushed northward along the border shared with Afghanistan—beginning in South Waziristan, then progressing through North Waziristan, into Bajur, and now reaching Swat and Buner. Beyond this territorial creep, the Taliban's influence has grown through alliances with terrorist factions based in Punjab province. These partnerships have enabled joint operations, including the assault on a Lahore police station. Compounding matters, Pakistani officials have repeatedly negotiated agreements with various Taliban-linked groups since the mid-2000s—arrangements that, rather than containing the militants, have actually facilitated their growth.

**Is Pakistan at risk of complete collapse?**

The short answer is no. That said, the Taliban's actions are compounding an already precarious political landscape. Pakistan's government, already fragile, contends with opposition from nearly every domestic political faction, not merely militant threats. Additionally, longstanding tensions with neighboring India force Pakistan to commit substantial military resources to that border, diverting attention and manpower away from counterterrorism efforts. While an outright Taliban takeover of Islamabad remains unlikely, continued militant assaults and territorial gains will progressively erode governmental stability, creating conditions in which the Taliban's influence could expand well beyond its current scope.

**What courses of action exist for Islamabad and the broader international community?**

Pakistan might benefit from establishing a coalition government representing diverse political interests, while simultaneously seeking greater international backing—particularly financial assistance and relaxed trade barriers to bolster its economy. Global powers could also play a role in mediating Pakistan's disputes with India, which would free up resources for internal governance and strengthen Pakistan's capacity to shape outcomes in neighboring Afghanistan.

Additionally, Pakistani leadership faces the challenge of persuading its citizenry that foreign assistance serves the nation's genuine interests in combating extremism and achieving stability. This requires securing backing from the sizable Pashtun population—a demographic from which the Taliban draws substantial recruitment. This task grows more complicated given that American military strikes in Pashtun territories, which continue to cause civilian casualties, undermine trust precisely as the U.S. is expected to serve as a key ally in Pakistan's stabilization efforts.

# The Expanding Taliban Threat in Pakistan: A Growing Crisis of State Stability

## The Northward March of Militancy

The Taliban's territorial influence has undergone a troubling geographic expansion along the Pakistan-Afghanistan border region. What began as a concentrated presence in South Waziristan has methodically spread northward, first into North Waziristan, then into the Bajur agency, and now encompasses the strategically significant districts of Swat and Buner. This progressive territorial acquisition represents more than mere geographic expansion—it signals a deepening entrenchment of militant infrastructure, governance structures, and operational capacity within Pakistan's tribal and settled areas. Each new territory brought under Taliban influence provides additional resources, recruitment opportunities, and staging grounds for further expansion, creating a cascading effect that has proven difficult for Pakistani authorities to contain.

## Strategic Alliances Extending Reach into Punjab

Perhaps most alarming has been the Taliban's success in forging strategic alliances with terrorist organizations based in Punjab, Pakistan's most populous and economically vital province. These partnerships have effectively extended the Taliban's operational reach far beyond the traditional tribal areas and into the heartland of Pakistani society. The assault on a police station in Lahore stands as a stark demonstration of this expanded capability—an attack that would have been unthinkable without the logistical support, local knowledge, and operational assistance provided by Punjab-based militant networks. This alliance-building strategy reveals a sophisticated approach by the Taliban to overcome geographic limitations and project power into areas previously considered insulated from tribal-based insurgency.

## The Unintended Consequences of Appeasement Policies

The roots of the current crisis can be traced back to a series of questionable policy decisions made by the Pakistani government beginning in 2004-2005. During this period, authorities repeatedly opted to negotiate settlements and cut deals with various Taliban-affiliated factions rather than pursuing sustained military or political confrontation. While these agreements may have offered short-term reductions in violence or bought temporary political breathing room, they ultimately proved counterproductive. Rather than containing the militant threat, these accommodations provided the Taliban with the time, space, and legitimacy needed to consolidate their position, reorganize their forces, and methodically extend their influence into new territories. This pattern of tactical concessions, repeated across multiple negotiations, effectively enabled the very expansion that Pakistani authorities were ostensibly trying to prevent.

## A Fragile State Under Multiple Pressures

Despite these serious challenges, the complete collapse of the Pakistani state remains an unlikely scenario. Pakistan possesses significant institutional resilience, a professional military establishment, and international support networks that provide some measure of stability. However, this does not diminish the severity of the current crisis. The Taliban's continued advances are placing additional strain on a government already contending with multiple simultaneous challenges: navigating complex relationships with numerous political parties, countering the growing militant threat, and managing persistent tensions with India along their shared border. This confluence of pressures creates a genuinely precarious situation, even if outright state failure is not imminent. The cumulative effect of these overlapping crises threatens to further erode governmental authority and public confidence in state institutions.

## Charting a Path Forward

Addressing this multifaceted crisis will require a comprehensive strategy that Pakistan cannot implement in isolation. Domestically, the formation of a broad-based government of national unity could provide the political cohesion necessary to mount an effective, sustained response to the Taliban threat—moving beyond the piecemeal and often contradictory policies that have characterized the government's approach in recent years. Such unity would help ensure consistent policy implementation across changing political administrations and reduce the vulnerability created by internal political fragmentation.

Simultaneously, increased international support will prove essential to Pakistan's ability to address these challenges effectively. This support should encompass expanded financial aid to help stabilize government finances and fund counter-insurgency efforts, as well as the lifting of trade restrictions that currently constrain Pakistan's economic development. A stronger Pakistani economy would not only improve living standards and reduce the socioeconomic conditions that make extremist recruitment more effective, but would also provide the government with greater resources and legitimacy to confront the Taliban threat directly. The international community's engagement, therefore, represents not merely humanitarian assistance but a strategic investment in regional stability that extends far beyond Pakistan's borders.

# The Expanding Taliban Threat in Pakistan

## Northward Expansion Along the Afghan Border

The Taliban's presence in Pakistan has undergone a significant transformation over the past several years, evolving from a localized insurgency concentrated in the tribal regions bordering Afghanistan into a broader, more geographically dispersed threat. Initially confined largely to the Federally Administered Tribal Areas (FATA) and parts of the North-West Frontier Province, Taliban militants have steadily pushed northward, extending their operational reach and territorial influence along the length of the Afghan border. This expansion has not occurred in isolation; it has been accompanied by the establishment of strategic alliances with terrorist organizations based in Punjab, Pakistan's most populous and politically significant province. These alliances have effectively created a networked insurgency that spans from the rugged tribal frontier deep into the Pakistani heartland, dramatically increasing the group's logistical capabilities, recruitment potential, and overall threat profile.

## The Role of Government Appeasement

A critical factor enabling this territorial and organizational expansion has been the Pakistani government's own policy choices. Beginning in 2004 and continuing through 2005 and beyond, various administrations—both military and civilian—entered into a series of peace deals and ceasefire agreements with different militant factions operating within the tribal areas. These agreements were often framed as pragmatic solutions to reduce immediate violence and buy time for broader counterterrorism strategies. However, in practice, they frequently had the opposite effect: rather than containing militant activity, these deals provided the Taliban and allied groups with breathing room to regroup, rearm, and reorganize. The ceasefires effectively ceded de facto control of certain territories to militant commanders, allowing them to establish parallel governance structures, training camps, and recruitment networks with minimal government interference. This pattern of appeasement, repeated across multiple agreements over several years, inadvertently facilitated the very expansion that Pakistani authorities were ostensibly trying to prevent.

## Assessing the Risk of State Collapse

Despite these troubling developments, most serious analysts and regional observers maintain that a complete collapse of the Pakistani state remains unlikely in the near to medium term. Pakistan possesses substantial military capacity, a functioning (if strained) civilian bureaucracy, and international backing that provides both material and diplomatic support. The country's nuclear arsenal, while raising separate security concerns, also ensures that international stakeholders remain deeply invested in preventing state failure. Nevertheless, the absence of total collapse should not be mistaken for stability or security. The Taliban's expanding influence represents a serious and compounding threat to an already fragile political and security architecture.

## Compounding Sources of Instability

Pakistan's vulnerability to Taliban expansion cannot be understood in isolation from the broader context of the country's internal political dysfunction. The government has long been beset by intense rivalries between competing political factions, military leadership, and civilian institutions, creating a fragmented decision-making environment ill-suited to mounting a coordinated response to militant expansion. These internal divisions often result in inconsistent policy implementation, with different factions within the security establishment and civilian government pursuing contradictory approaches toward militant groups—some favoring negotiation and accommodation, others advocating for aggressive military action.

Compounding this internal political fragility is the persistent and unresolved tension along Pakistan's eastern border with India. This long-standing rivalry forces Pakistani military planners to divide their attention and resources between two very different security challenges: a conventional (and potentially nuclear) standoff with India to the east, and an increasingly sophisticated insurgency along the western border with Afghanistan. This dual-front strategic burden stretches Pakistan's military and intelligence resources thin, limiting the government's capacity to mount a fully resourced and sustained campaign against Taliban expansion in the north and west.

## The Path Forward: International Support and Domestic Unity

Given these compounding pressures, the trajectory of Taliban influence in Pakistan will likely be determined by two critical factors moving forward. First, sustained international support—encompassing military assistance, intelligence sharing, economic aid, and diplomatic engagement—will be essential in providing Pakistan with the resources and strategic partnerships necessary to counter militant expansion effectively. Without this external support, Pakistan's ability to simultaneously manage its internal insurgency and external border tensions would be severely compromised.

Second, and perhaps more importantly, the emergence of a unified and coherent Pakistani government will be crucial to translating available resources into effective action. Political infighting and institutional fragmentation have historically undermined even well-resourced counterterrorism initiatives, as competing factions pursue divergent strategies or actively obstruct one another's efforts. Only through greater political cohesion—bridging the divides between civilian leadership, military command, and intelligence services—can Pakistan hope to present a unified front against the Taliban's continued expansion.

Absent progress on these two fronts, the risk is not necessarily state collapse, but rather a continued gradual erosion of governmental authority in ever-widening swaths of Pakistani territory, with the Taliban and its allied networks filling the resulting power vacuum. This scenario would have profound implications not only for Pakistan's internal stability but for regional security more broadly, given Pakistan's strategic importance, nuclear capabilities, and central role in the broader struggle against militant extremism in South Asia.

# CNN Coverage of the Taliban's Influence in Pakistan

CNN has extensively covered the complex relationship between the Taliban and Pakistan, a topic that remains central to understanding regional security dynamics in South Asia. This coverage spans multiple dimensions of a relationship that has evolved significantly since the Taliban's resurgence in Afghanistan.

## Historical Context

Pakistan's relationship with the Taliban dates back to the 1990s, when Pakistani intelligence services were reported to have supported the group during its rise to power in Afghanistan. This historical connection has made Pakistan a focal point for international media coverage, including CNN's reporting, particularly regarding allegations of continued support or influence.

## Post-2021 Developments

Following the Taliban's return to power in Kabul in August 2021, CNN has reported extensively on how this shift affected Pakistan's security situation. Key areas of coverage include:

**Cross-border militancy**: Reports have focused on the Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), a separate but ideologically aligned group that has intensified attacks within Pakistan, straining relations between Islamabad and the Afghan Taliban government.

**Diplomatic tensions**: CNN has covered the deteriorating relationship between Pakistan and the Afghan Taliban, despite historical ties, as Pakistani officials have accused Afghan authorities of harboring militants responsible for attacks on Pakistani soil.

**Refugee and border issues**: Coverage has included Pakistan's controversial deportation of Afghan refugees and the humanitarian implications of these policies.

**Security incidents**: Regular reporting on terrorist attacks, military operations, and casualties resulting from the ongoing militant activity in Pakistan's border regions, particularly in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan provinces.

## Broader Implications

CNN's coverage often situates these developments within larger geopolitical contexts, examining how the Taliban-Pakistan relationship affects:

- Regional stability in South Asia
- International counterterrorism efforts
- Pakistan's internal political and economic challenges
- Diplomatic relations with other nations, including the United States, China, and India

This ongoing coverage reflects the complex, sometimes contradictory nature of Pakistan-Taliban relations, which have shifted from alleged strategic support to growing security concerns as militant violence has increased within Pakistani territory itself.

# The Shadow War: How Taliban Influence Is Reshaping Pakistan's Security Landscape

*A CNN International Correspondent Analysis*

---

**ISLAMABAD** — In a wide-ranging discussion on the deteriorating security situation along Pakistan's western frontier, CNN correspondent analysis reveals a complex web of militant resurgence, governmental strain, and diplomatic hesitation that is reshaping South Asian geopolitics.

**The Interview**

*CNN Anchor:* You've just returned from the border regions. What's the situation on the ground?

*Correspondent:* What we're witnessing is fundamentally different from the Taliban threat of a decade ago. The Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan, or TTP, has capitalized on the Afghan Taliban's 2021 takeover of Kabul. There's a psychological and logistical dimension here — sanctuary across the border, ideological reinforcement, and in some cases, materiel that's flowed through porous frontier crossings.

Local officials in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and parts of Balochistan describe a shadow governance structure emerging in certain districts — parallel courts, taxation systems, and intimidation campaigns against government officials who don't comply.

*Anchor:* How has Islamabad responded?

*Correspondent:* Pakistan's response has been notably inconsistent. There was an initial period of cautious optimism after the Afghan Taliban's return to power — a belief in Islamabad that ideological kinship might translate into cooperation against the TTP. That calculation has largely failed. Kabul has been unwilling or unable to rein in TTP fighters operating from Afghan soil.

We've seen Pakistan's military conduct cross-border airstrikes, which Kabul has condemned as violations of sovereignty. Meanwhile, domestically, there's friction between the civilian government and military establishment over strategy — some officials favor negotiation, others insist only sustained kinetic operations will work.

**The International Dimension**

*Anchor:* Where does this leave the international community?

*Correspondent:* That's the critical question, and frankly, the response has been fragmented. The United States remains focused on counterterrorism concerns but has limited appetite for renewed military engagement in the region. Washington's leverage has diminished considerably since the 2021 withdrawal.

China has significant economic interests through CPEC — the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor — and has quietly pressured Islamabad for better security guarantees for Chinese nationals, several of whom have been targeted in attacks.

*Anchor:* What options realistically exist?

*Correspondent:* Analysts I've spoken with outline several tracks. First, intelligence-sharing arrangements — multilateral frameworks involving Pakistan, Gulf states, and Western partners to track financing and recruitment networks. Second, targeted economic assistance conditioned on governance reforms in frontier regions, addressing the root grievances that make these areas vulnerable to militant recruitment.

Third — and this is contentious — some voices are calling for renewed diplomatic engagement with the Afghan Taliban itself, using economic incentives and recognition as leverage to pressure them on TTP sanctuary. Critics argue this legitimizes a government with a deeply troubling human rights record, particularly regarding women's rights.

*Anchor:* Is there consensus on the way forward?

*Correspondent:* Honestly, no. There's tension between those prioritizing immediate counterterrorism cooperation and those insisting any engagement must be conditioned on humanitarian benchmarks. What's clear is that without a coordinated regional approach — one that includes Iran, the Central Asian states, and doesn't solely rely on Pakistani unilateral action — this problem will likely metastasize rather than resolve.

---

*This analysis reflects ongoing reporting and should be considered alongside developing situations on the ground.*

counterfactuals.output:
# The Taliban's Expansion from Waziristan to Swat and Buner

This is a critical question in Pakistan's security history, particularly relevant to the 2007-2009 period when this expansion became most alarming to analysts. Let me break down the dynamics experts identified, while being clear about the limits of any single narrative.

## The Pattern of Expansion

**From FATA to "Settled Areas"**

Experts like Ahmed Rashid and analysts at the International Crisis Group described a deliberate strategy:

- **Waziristan as base**: The Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), formed under Baitullah Mehsud in 2007, used North and South Waziristan as sanctuary, benefiting from tribal autonomy, difficult terrain, and porous ties to Afghan Taliban networks.

- **Swat as testing ground**: Maulana Fazlullah's movement in Swat (2007-2009) showed how militants could exploit a settled district—not tribal agency—using local grievances (slow justice system, resentment of feudal elites, FM radio propaganda) to build genuine local support before imposing control through violence.

- **Buner as strategic leap**: The 2009 advance into Buner alarmed observers precisely because it was adjacent to Islamabad-Peshawar corridor, suggesting militants were testing whether the state would respond to encroachment beyond "tribal" areas into Pakistan's political heartland.

**Mechanisms experts cited:**
- Exploitation of weak governance and slow judicial systems
- Use of madrassas and FM radio for recruitment/propaganda
- Assassination of rival tribal elders/maliks who might resist
- Peace deals (like the 2009 Swat agreement allowing Sharia courts) that critics argued gave militants time to regroup rather than genuinely pacifying areas

## The "Failed State" Debate

This is where I should flag significant disagreement among experts rather than presenting one verdict:

**Arguments for serious concern:**
- Analysts like Bruce Riedel warned of a nuclear-armed state with expanding ungoverned space
- The Swat deal was seen by some as evidence the state was ceding sovereignty rather than defeating insurgents
- Weak civilian institutions, ISI's historically ambivalent relationship with some militant groups, and economic strain fed pessimism

**Arguments against the "failed state" framing:**
- Pakistan retained a large, functioning military, intact state institutions, and (unlike classic failed states) never lost control of its major cities or nuclear command structure
- The 2009 Swat military operation demonstrated the state *could* mobilize significant force when it chose to
- Scholars like Anatol Lieven cautioned against catastrophizing, arguing Pakistan's resilience—messy democracy, army cohesion, social structures—was underestimated

## Where I'd Push Back on the Framing

The "failed state" label is often more rhetorically powerful than analytically precise. It conflates:
1. **Governance failures** in specific regions (real, significant)
2. **State collapse** (didn't occur—Pakistan retained core sovereignty, military capacity, and international functioning)

Experts like Lieven argued Pakistan was better understood as a state with serious **capacity gaps in peripheral governance**, not a state on the verge of collapse. The subsequent military operations (Rah-e-Rast in Swat, 2009; Zarb-e-Azb in Waziristan, 2014) demonstrated the state's ability to reassert control militarily, even if political/governance solutions remained incomplete.

**Bottom line**: The expansion reflected genuine governance vulnerabilities Pakistan needed to address urgently, but "failed state" predictions from 2009 proved overstated—the state didn't collapse, though the human and political costs of the conflict were severe and enduring.

# A Conversation on Pakistan's Instability: Regional Dynamics and the Path Forward

*The following is an illustrative Q&A exploring the complex security challenges facing Pakistan, framed as an interview with a senior international correspondent covering South Asian affairs.*

---

**Q: Let's start with the fundamentals. How would you characterize Pakistan's current instability?**

A: Pakistan is dealing with layered crises that compound one another. You have economic distress—debt burdens, currency pressure, and dependence on IMF support. You have political fragmentation following years of contested elections and tension between civilian governments and the military establishment. And overlaying all of this is a resurgent security threat, particularly along the Afghan border, where militant groups have expanded their operational reach. None of these problems exist in isolation; economic desperation feeds recruitment into militancy, and political instability weakens the state's capacity to respond coherently.

**Q: You mentioned militant expansion. What's happening with groups like the Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP)?**

A: Since the Afghan Taliban's return to power in Kabul in 2021, the TTP has felt emboldened. There's ideological kinship and, many analysts believe, sanctuary and logistical support flowing across the border. The TTP has intensified attacks in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and parts of Balochistan, targeting security forces and, increasingly, civilians. This isn't full territorial control in the conventional sense—it's more accurately described as expanding influence, contested zones, and a breakdown of state authority in certain districts rather than the Taliban literally annexing land. But the psychological and strategic effect is significant: it signals that Islamabad cannot fully secure its own frontier.

**Q: Why hasn't the relationship between Islamabad and the Afghan Taliban translated into better security cooperation, given Pakistan's historical support for the Afghan Taliban?**

A: That's the irony many people miss. Pakistan spent decades cultivating relationships with Afghan Taliban factions, expecting a friendly or at least neutral government in Kabul. Instead, the Afghan Taliban has shown reluctance to crack down on the TTP, partly due to shared ideology, partly due to internal Taliban politics, and partly because expelling fighters could destabilize their own fragile control over Afghanistan. Pakistan essentially miscalculated—it got a neighbor sympathetic to militants it now needs suppressed.

**Q: Turning to potential solutions—what role could the United States realistically play?**

A: Washington's leverage is more limited than it once was, given the withdrawal in 2021 and reduced strategic appetite for deep involvement in the region. That said, the U.S. retains tools: intelligence sharing, counterterrorism cooperation, economic assistance tied to reform, and diplomatic pressure on both Islamabad and, indirectly, Kabul. Some analysts argue for a recalibrated relationship—less about broad strategic partnership and more targeted, transactional cooperation on specific threats like ISIS-K and TTP, which threaten U.S. interests too. The challenge is trust deficits on both sides after years of mutual frustration.

**Q: And India? That's a more complicated relationship given the history with Pakistan.**

A: It is complicated, but not irrelevant. Some regional security analysts propose that India and Pakistan share a genuine mutual interest in containing cross-border militancy, even if they'll never say so warmly in public. Track-two diplomacy—backchannel discussions between former officials and analysts—has occasionally floated ideas around intelligence cooperation on specific terrorist networks. Realistically, though, the Kashmir dispute and decades of mistrust make formal cooperation politically toxic in both capitals. Any progress would likely be quiet, incremental, and deniable rather than a public partnership.

**Q: Is there a scenario where these external actors actually stabilize the situation, or is this fundamentally a problem Pakistan has to solve internally?**

A: I'd lean toward the latter, with caveats. External actors can provide resources, intelligence, and diplomatic pressure, but they can't substitute for functional governance. Pakistan needs coherent civil-military coordination, economic reforms that reduce the desperation driving recruitment, and a border strategy that doesn't rely solely on military operations, which have historically displaced populations without eliminating underlying grievances. The U.S. and India can be part of a supporting architecture, but expecting them to solve what is fundamentally a crisis of state capacity and internal cohesion is unrealistic.

**Q: Final question—what's the timeline here? Are we looking at gradual deterioration or something more acute?**

A: I'd caution against dramatic predictions of imminent collapse—Pakistan has weathered severe crises before. But the trajectory over the next few years matters enormously. If economic conditions don't stabilize and militant attacks continue escalating, you risk a slow erosion of state authority in border regions that becomes very difficult to reverse. The window for course correction likely narrows the longer these overlapping crises go unaddressed.

---

*Note: This piece presents an illustrative analytical framework based on publicly reported dynamics in the region as of recent years. Specific assessments should be verified against current reporting, as the security situation evolves rapidly.*

# Pakistan's Security Crisis Deepens as Militant Networks Converge

*Analysis*

**ISLAMABAD** — Pakistan's security establishment faces a mounting challenge as intelligence assessments and regional analysts point to deepening cooperation between Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) and militant networks historically based in Punjab province, complicating an already fraught counterterrorism landscape.

## A Shifting Threat Picture

For years, Pakistani security officials drew a rough distinction between groups focused on the Afghan border regions and those—often referred to as "Punjab-based" militant outfits—with roots in sectarian and anti-India militancy, some of which had historical ties to state intelligence services during the 1980s and 1990s. That distinction, analysts say, has eroded.

Groups such as factions linked to Jaish-e-Mohammed and Lashkar-e-Jhangvi have reportedly provided fighters, logistical support, and safe havens to TTP-aligned militants operating in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and the former tribal areas. This convergence reflects both ideological alignment post-2021 Taliban takeover in Afghanistan and practical necessity, as militant groups pool resources amid sustained military pressure.

"What we're seeing is a blurring of lines that Pakistani security planners spent decades trying to maintain," said one regional security analyst who tracks militant financing networks. "When groups share trainers, weapons pipelines, and ideological messaging, the old categories stop being useful."

## Why This Matters Now

The stakes have risen sharply since the Taliban's return to power in Kabul in August 2021. Islamabad had hoped a friendly government in Afghanistan would pressure TTP fighters sheltering there. Instead, Pakistani officials have repeatedly accused Kabul of tolerating—if not actively enabling—TTP sanctuary, straining bilateral relations to their lowest point in years.

Cross-border attacks have surged, particularly in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan, with Pakistani military casualties climbing. The involvement of fighters and facilitators from Punjab-based networks adds a dimension that complicates Pakistan's traditional playbook, which relied on distinguishing "good" and "bad" militants based on their targets.

## Islamabad's Narrowing Options

Pakistan's government and military face a limited menu of choices, each carrying significant risk:

**Military escalation.** Continued or expanded operations in the former tribal districts risk displacing civilian populations again, echoing the humanitarian toll of earlier campaigns like Zarb-e-Azb. Renewed large-scale displacement could also fuel local resentment that militants exploit.

**Diplomatic pressure on Kabul.** Islamabad has pushed the Taliban government to act against TTP sanctuaries, including through periodic border closures and, reportedly, limited airstrikes inside Afghan territory. These moves have yielded little visible change in TTP capability and have further poisoned Pakistan-Afghanistan relations.

**Negotiation.** Islamabad previously experimented with talks and even resettlement of some TTP fighters, an approach widely criticized after it appeared to embolden militants rather than de-escalate violence. Renewed dialogue remains politically toxic domestically.

**Dismantling domestic militant infrastructure.** Addressing the Punjab-based networks would require confronting groups with longstanding, complex relationships to elements of the security establishment—a politically sensitive undertaking that previous governments have approached unevenly.

**Regional and international cooperation.** Pakistan has sought closer coordination with China, Gulf partners, and Western counterterrorism agencies, though experts note that external support cannot substitute for domestic policy clarity.

## The Bottom Line

Analysts broadly agree that Pakistan's security challenge is no longer confined to its western border regions but reflects an interconnected militant ecosystem spanning provinces and, in the TTP's case, an international border. Addressing it will likely require Islamabad to make politically difficult choices about long-tolerated domestic networks—choices successive governments have deferred.

Without a coherent strategy addressing both the Afghan sanctuary question and domestic militant infrastructure, security officials and independent analysts warn, Pakistan risks a prolonged period of instability that could strain its military, economy, and already fragile civil-military relations.

---

*This analysis draws on publicly available assessments from regional security researchers and reporting on Pakistan's counterterrorism posture. CNN has sought comment from Pakistan's Ministry of Interior and Inter-Services Public Relations.*
